name: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
title: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
answer: Vector search stores embeddings, which are lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables. That means retrieval can respect the same joins, filters, and permissions as the rest of the data. The scope covers similarity search over text, images, audio, or any other item that has been embedded. It also covers hybrid queries that combine vector distance with ordinary SQL predicates.

sections.body: Vector search stores embeddings, which are lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables. That means retrieval can respect the same joins, filters, and permissions as the rest of the data. The scope covers similarity search over text, images, audio, or any other item that has been embedded. It also covers hybrid queries that combine vector distance with ordinary SQL predicates.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: It runs inside the database server process, using the same storage engine, buffer pool, write-ahead log, and replication path as ordinary tables. A vector column is just another column type, so backups, point-in-time recovery, and read replicas apply to it. Indexes for nearest neighbor search, such as HNSW or IVFFlat, are built and maintained by the database. No separate vector service is required, though many deployments still call an embedding model to produce the vectors before they are inserted.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with an embedding model that turns text, images, or other items into vectors. Those vectors are written to a column in a relational table, next to the original row. A query is embedded the same way, then the database orders rows by a distance measure such as cosine or Euclidean distance and returns the nearest ones. Because the search is a SQL query, it can be filtered by tenant, joined to other tables, and paginated like any other result set. Approximate indexes trade a little recall for speed, and exact search is used when the dataset is small or recall must be perfect.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because vectors live in the same database, existing access controls, row-level security, and audit logs can apply to them. That helps keep retrieval within the same permission model as the source data, but it also means a vector column inherits the sensitivity of the rows it sits beside. Provenance matters: teams need to record which embedding model produced a vector, when, and from what source text or media. Embeddings can sometimes be inverted or used to infer attributes, so they are not automatically safe to expose. Retention, deletion, and subject access requests must cover the vectors as well as the original records.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Vector search inside SQL databases is moving from a niche extension to a standard feature of relational engines. More databases are adding native vector types, distance operators, and approximate indexes. The likely direction is tighter integration with query planners, so a single SQL statement can mix relational filters, full-text search, and vector similarity. Agent frameworks and Model Context Protocol servers are also making database retrieval a common tool call, and this site tracks 263 such servers for SQL databases and warehouses. The open questions are around index maintenance, cost control, and how to keep embeddings fresh as data changes.
